transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-21 15:00 PDT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Amir Patel (CTO, Krypton Health), Laura Ng (ML Eng Lead), Sam Ortiz (Infra Manager), Heather Kim (PM)

Auto-summary (auto):
- High level discovery on unit economics: per-token pricing vs per-request cost, batching/caching levers, Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private VPC tradeoffs.
- Customer to share token histogram and sample queries. Redwood to send tailored price model and run Dedicated benchmark.

Topics: pricing, batching, KV/prefix caching, latency SLOs, dedicated commits, private deployment costs, SOC2/KMS questions.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intro — I’m Maya, AE on the account, Diego and Priya from our SE team. How are we doing?
[00:06] Amir (Krypton): Good, thanks. We have a short agenda — mostly economics and deployment options. We want to understand what we'll pay and how to keep costs predictable.
[00:12] Maya: Perfect. Laura, Amir, Sam — can you give a 2-minute overview of the stack and the volume profiles you're expecting?
[00:20] Laura (Krypton): Sure. We're doing clinical note summarization and a triage assistant. Typical prompt length is 300-800 tokens, response 80-300 tokens. Peak concurrent sessions maybe 500-700 active users, but queries are bursty — a couple spikes daily. Overall monthly active usage estimates: around 120M tokens/month to start, can double in 6 months. Budget is...tight. We want to keep average cost per user under, like, $0.50/month for the MVP.
[00:42] Diego (Redwood): Got it. That's helpful. With a hosted per-token model, rough math: if you average 400 tokens in+out per request, at $0.0003/token that's about $0.12 per request, so you can see where it grows. But batching and KV/prefix caching can cut effective tokens per request or amortize GPU cost.
[01:05] Amir: When you say batching, is that server-side automatic or something we configure? We can't have increased latency for doctors.
[01:11] Priya (Redwood): It's workload-aware. Redwood's runtime does continuous batching where it groups similar in-flight requests — that can reduce GPU cycles. We expose tuning knobs: max latency target, batch windows. For low-latency SLOs (sub-200ms), you'll get smaller batches; 200-500ms SLOs allow more aggressive batching and bigger savings.
[01:35] Sam (Krypton): For triage, 200-300ms is okay. For note generation, 800-1000ms okay. Can we split routes?
[01:42] Diego: Absolutely — per-route SLOs + different model variants. We often route latency-sensitive endpoints to Hosted low-latency pool or Dedicated with reserved GPUs; heavy generation can go to cheaper variants or quantized instances.
[01:55] Heather (Krypton): What's the delta between Hosted and Dedicated on unit token cost? Give a ballpark.
[02:02] Maya: Depends on commit size and model. Example: for a 3B-ish open model on Hosted, list per-token might be $0.00025 inbound + $0.00035 outbound (we bill combined effective). Dedicated amortizes GPU infra and gives lower per-token at scale — maybe 30-50% lower unit cost for steady state if you commit and time-share efficiently. But Dedicated has monthly reserved cost plus minimum commit.
[02:29] Amir: So if we're at 120M tokens, Dedicated might not make sense until we double?
[02:34] Diego: Correct, typical break-even depends on model and burst patterns. If you have predictable sustained baseline, Dedicated often wins. If bursts are unpredictable, Hosted + burst/dedicated hybrid can be good — Redwood Dedicated supports autoscale and burst capacity on top of reserved pools.
[02:51] Laura: Tell us more about caching. We get lots of repeated prefixes — templates. How much can that save us?
[02:57] Priya: Prefix/KV caching is very effective for clinical templates. If 30% of requests share a long prefix, you can cache the KV cache layer so the runtime reuses past attention keys; that reduces compute per token dramatically. Typical observed savings: 20-60% depending on prompt reuse. In some cases with high prefix reuse we saw effective token compute drop by 70% for outbound tokens.
[03:20] Amir: Is that something we maintain, or is it automatic? Also, how long is the cache kept?
[03:25] Diego: It's configurable. You can set TTLs per route and also pin keys for session-based reuse. For PHI-sensitive content we support encrypted KVs and you control retention via config and policy.
[03:37] Sam: Encryption — does that meet our KMS/HSM requirements? We need keys not accessible to Redwood ops.
[03:43] Maya: For Private deployments we can integrate with customer KMS/HSM. For Hosted, we offer customer-managed keys via supported cloud KMS for encryption-at-rest of cached artifacts and logs; some customers prefer Private for full control. We'll include the security doc.
[03:56] Heather: We need SOC2 and ISO stuff.
[03:58] Maya: Redwood's hosted control plane is SOC 2 Type II; Private deployments let you keep the control plane in your VPC and meet stricter audit needs. We'll attach our compliance pack.
[04:08] Amir: Back to costs — what levers should we prioritize? Batching, cache, model size, quantization?
[04:14] Diego: Order-of-impact often: caching (if your workload has reuse), model size/architecture (smaller models are cheaper), quantization (int8 or int4 reduces memory footprint and cost but may have slight quality impact), and batching. Also route-level sampling and reranking to avoid hitting largest models for every request.
[04:31] Laura: Have you done any head-to-head on quality loss with int4 quantization for clinical summarization?
[04:36] Priya: We have benchmarks. For many encoder-decoder summarization tasks, int8 has negligible degradation; int4 sometimes shows edge-case phrasing issues. With Redwood Optimize we can run evals on your prompt set to measure regression and only apply quantization where acceptable.
[04:50] Amir: If we do a pilot, what's the smallest dedicated commit we should consider?
[04:55] Diego: We usually see customers start with a small Dedicated slab — e.g., 1-2 A100-equivalent GPUs reserved for baseline traffic plus burst to Hosted. That lowers tail latency and gives a good baseline to instrument economics. But commits can be monthly and are negotiable.
[05:11] Maya: We'll include a modeled example in the spreadsheet: scenario A (Hosted-only), scenario B (Hybrid with 2-GPU Dedicated), scenario C (Private on-prem). We'll show per-token, infra amortized, and net monthly cost given your 120M token baseline.
[05:25] Laura: In terms of observability — can we get token-level cost and traces per tenant? We need per-customer attribution for billing.
[05:32] Maya: Yes, Redwood Console exposes per-token cost breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and you can export cost attribution by API keys or tenant tags.
[05:40] Sam: Any gotchas on token counting? We want deterministic billing for internal chargeback.
[05:44] Diego: We bill based on model tokenizer tokens measured on the server side; we provide a tokenization preview tool. Note edge cases like whitespace differences between client and server tokenizers — we recommend using our SDK tokenizers in preflight to match billing.
[05:59] Heather: What about cold start or model load times — if we move to Dedicated, are there model load charges when spinning new variant?
[06:06] Diego: Model warmup is part of the Dedicated pool. If you spin up additional replicas beyond reserved capacity, there may be transient costs. We expose options: keep a warm standby replica (small monthly cost) to avoid model load latency, or accept a few seconds load time for new scale-outs.
[06:22] Amir: For our SLA, 99.9% is desirable. What does that imply for architecture?
[06:27] Maya: For 99.9%, multi-AZ Dedicated pools or Hosted redundancy across regions is recommended, plus automatic fallback to smaller models. We can draft an architecture diagram in the follow up.
[06:36] Laura: Any compliance concerns using caching with PHI? We need to be able to opt-out or minimize retention per profile.
[06:42] Priya: Yes — you can set route-level retention to zero and avoid caching for PHI workflows, or use per-tenant encryption and very short TTLs. Private deployment gives more control if you need absolute isolation.
[06:54] Amir: Pricing — can you walk through an example with numbers? Like per 1M tokens.
[06:58] Maya: Sure. Example ballparks (public examples, will send spreadsheet): Hosted (3B model): $2.50 - $3.50 per 1M tokens effective depending on in/out split and model. With heavy quantization/Dedicated + cache we can drop to $1.50 per 1M tokens effective at scale. So on 120M tokens that's roughly $180-$420/mo Hosted, or $180-$300 with optimizations. These are illustrative; we'll tailor.
[07:25] Sam: That Hosted number seems lower than what we feared — are there hidden costs?
[07:29] Maya: Good callout. The listed numbers exclude optional add-ons like retention beyond default, advanced observability retention, and private deployment licensing. Also egress or custom KMS connectors with third-party costs. We'll annotate each line.
[07:43] Laura: How do you show the savings from batching in the spreadsheet?
[07:46] Diego: We'll model effective throughput improvement and show two curves: latency-targeted batch config (low-latency, low batch savings) and cost-targeted (higher latency tolerance, higher batch savings). We'll show expected percent token compute saved per scenario and converted to $/1M tokens.
[08:01] Heather: For the pilot, we want to test real queries. Can Redwood run an evaluation with our dataset?
[08:06] Priya: Yes. We'll run a benchmark on your sample corpus to measure latency, cost per output token under different quantization and batch settings. We'll produce a report.
[08:15] Amir: Timeline-wise, we'd like pilot started mid-September. Are there any lead times for Dedicated?
[08:20] Diego: Dedicated provisioning can be quick (days) for modest capacity but depends on region. We'll aim to have a bench environment ready by 2025-09-08 if we get samples by 2025-08-27.
[08:31] Maya: I'll send the pricing spreadsheet and a checklist of artifacts we need. Diego will own the benchmark setup.
[08:36] Sam: One more: Do you support per-tenant rate limits and burst controls? We need to throttle certain enterprise clients.
[08:42] Priya: Yes, per-API-key rate limits, quotas, and token caps per tenant with alerting.
[08:47] Laura: Any references or case studies in health?
[08:50] Maya: We have a few anonymized health customers; I'll include one pager. Also we'll attach our SOC2 and security whitepaper.
[08:58] Amir: Great. For decision criteria — we'll evaluate on (1) cost per 1k active users, (2) latency at P95, (3) compliance fit, (4) pilot results.
[09:08] Maya: Understood. We'll map those into the spreadsheet and propose success criteria.
[09:12] Heather: If we move to Private later, what's the migration complexity?
[09:16] Diego: We've migrated customers from Hosted to Private with minimal API changes — same endpoints, config differences. Migration usually involves network setup (VPC peering), KMS integration, and a short re-deploy window. We'll provide a runbook.
[09:30] Amir: Any final notes on cost levers we should internalize?
[09:33] Diego: Short list: 1) reduce model size where acceptable, 2) use caching for templates, 3) set per-route latency-cost tradeoffs, 4) quantize selectively after evaluation, 5) use Dedicated for steady baseline and Hosted for burst.
[09:48] Maya: Ok — recap of next steps: Maya send pricing + compliance docs; Diego set up benchmark template; Krypton provide token histograms and sample queries; schedule pilot bench first week of September.
[09:58] Amir: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[10:01] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invites and links.
[10:05] End of recording.

Shared artifacts referenced: pricing spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.example.com/links/pricing-krypton), security pack (link: https://redwood.example.com/links/security-pack), Dedicated benchmark template (note: will be shared by Diego).

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard words (K-V / KV cache), some speaker overlap near end.
